meta.title: Homeostasis
meta.summary: Your outside world swings wildly — cold nights, hot afternoons, huge meals, days without food. Your inside world barely moves at all.

sections.title: Homeostatic Control Systems — The Machinery Behind the Constancy
Signal Transduction — How Cells Hear the Message
Classic Examples of Homeostasis in Action

items: Your outside world swings wildly — cold nights, hot afternoons, huge meals, days without food. Your inside world barely moves at all.
That stubborn steadiness is homeostasis, and it is not luck: it is thousands of little control loops correcting you every second.
Every loop has the same three parts — a sensor, a control centre, and an effector. Learn the pattern once and you can predict almost any regulatory system in the body.
The whole thing is best understood as a thermostat, repeated everywhere — for temperature, sugar, water, salt, pH and pressure.
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment, despite whatever the outside world is doing.
Stable does not mean frozen. Values drift up and down constantly around a set point — they are just never allowed to drift far. Think of a tightrope walker: never still, never falling.
The 'internal environment' is a real, specific thing: the ECF — the fluid actually bathing your cells. Cells never touch the outside world; they only ever experience the ECF.
The variables defended include temperature, glucose, oxygen and CO₂, pH, ions, blood pressure and osmolarity.
Claude Bernard described the constant internal environment (milieu intérieur); Walter Cannon named it homeostasis.
When a loop fails, the result is not a small inconvenience — it is disease. Most illness is homeostasis losing an argument.
An air conditioner holding a room at 24 °C: it does not hold the room perfectly still, it keeps overshooting slightly and correcting. That is homeostasis exactly.
You can walk from a cold air-conditioned lecture hall into blazing afternoon sun and your core temperature moves by a fraction of a degree — the whole adjustment happens invisibly.

blocks.x: Imagine a thermostat in a house. No matter if it's freezing or blazing outside, the thermostat keeps the inside temperature steady by switching the heater or AC on and off. Your body does the exact same thing, but for dozens of variables at once — temperature, pH, oxygen, sugar, salt — all held remarkably constant no matter what's happening in the world around you. That is homeostasis.

blocks.name: Homeostasis (definition)
blocks.def: The maintenance of a constant, relatively stable internal environment in the face of a constantly changing external environment. Simple version: keeping the inside steady while the outside is chaos.

blocks.name: Claude Bernard
blocks.def: The physiologist who created the underlying concept in 1878, proposing the principle of the constancy of the 'milieu intérieur' (internal environment). He explained that the living body, though dependent on its surroundings, is relatively independent of them because its tissues are protected by an internal environment made up of the fluids circulating through the body.

blocks.name: Walter Cannon
blocks.def: Coined the actual term 'homeostasis' in 1932, from the Greek words homeo (same, similar) and stasis (standing still, staying changeless). Bernard had the idea; Cannon gave it its name.

blocks.name: The internal environment = the ECF
blocks.def: The <term d="All the body fluid sitting outside the cells, including blood plasma and the fluid bathing tissues.">extracellular fluid</term> (ECF) is considered to BE the body's internal environment — this is the fluid that Bernard was describing, the fluid that bathes every cell and must be kept constant.

blocks.name: The essential variables kept within limits
blocks.def: Concentration of oxygen and carbon dioxide, pH of the internal environment, concentration of nutrients and waste products, concentration of salt and other electrolytes, volume and pressure of extracellular fluid, and temperature. These are the 'dashboard readouts' the body is constantly monitoring and correcting.

blocks.name: Homeostatic imbalance
blocks.def: A condition where homeostasis is disturbed — much of disease is, at its root, a disturbance of homeostasis. This is exactly why understanding homeostasis is the basis for clinical diagnosis: doctors are often literally looking for which homeostatic variable has gone out of range.

blocks.name: Body systems supporting homeostasis
blocks.def: Homeostasis depends on the coordinated action of many organ systems: integumentary, circulatory, lymphatic/immune, digestive, nervous, <term d="Signalling in which hormones travel through the bloodstream to reach distant target cells.">endocrine</term>, reproductive, muscular, skeletal, respiratory, and excretory. It takes the whole body working together, not one organ alone.

blocks.name: The two main control systems of homeostasis
blocks.def: The nervous system and, to a lesser degree, the endocrine system are the main control systems of homeostasis — nerves for fast, moment-to-moment correction; hormones for slower, longer-lasting correction.

blocks.name: Why homeostasis matters evolutionarily
blocks.def: Homeostasis allows humans to live in many different habitats — from the Arctic to the desert — because the internal environment stays the same no matter how extreme the external environment gets.

sections.title: Homeostatic Control Systems — The Machinery Behind the Constancy

items: Three parts, always: sensor (receptor) detects the change → control centre compares it against the set point → effector does something about it.
Negative feedback is the workhorse: the response opposes the change. Too hot → cool down. Too much sugar → store it. It is self-limiting, so it settles.
Positive feedback does the opposite: the response amplifies the change, driving it faster. It cannot be used casually — it needs a definite end point or it runs away.
Feedforward is the clever one: the body acts before the disturbance arrives, using a warning signal rather than waiting for the damage.
Simple test to tell them apart: ask 'does the response cancel the change or add to it?'
Your mouth waters at the smell of food, before a bite is taken — feedforward, preparing digestion in advance.
Your heart rate rises on the starting line, before you have run a single step — again feedforward, not a reaction to exertion that has not happened yet.
Shivering when cold and sweating when hot are the two most obvious negative feedback loops you own.

blocks.x: Every homeostatic control system works like a simple three-part team: someone who notices the problem, someone who decides what to do about it, and someone who actually does it. Miss any one part and the whole system fails.

blocks.cap: The <term d="A control loop where the response reverses the original change, pulling the body back to normal.">negative feedback</term> loop that underlies most homeostatic regulation.

blocks.name: Homeostatic control systems (definition)
blocks.def: Body components that generate compensatory regulatory responses to maintain relatively stable conditions of the internal environment. They are subject to nervous and endocrine control.

blocks.name: The three components of a homeostatic control system
blocks.def: Detectors/sensors (notice the change), an integrating/control center (decides what to do), and effectors (carry out the response). Memory hook: Sense it, Decide it, Fix it.

blocks.name: Two basic strategies for maintaining homeostasis
blocks.def: Feedback and feedforward — feedback reacts AFTER a change has happened, feedforward acts BEFORE a change happens, anticipating it.

blocks.name: Feedback control (general)
blocks.def: The course of a reaction is controlled by the activity of some of the products of that very reaction — in other words, a mechanism where the products of a process become the regulators of that same process. Feedback control can be negative or positive.

blocks.name: Negative feedback
blocks.def: Occurs when a change in a controlled variable triggers a response that OPPOSES that change — pushing the variable back toward normal. This is the principle homeostasis primarily runs on. Negative feedback mechanisms are inhibitory and help maintain equilibrium; disrupting negative feedback can lead to undesirable, often dangerous, results. Simple analogy: a thermostat cooling the room down BECAUSE it got too hot.

blocks.name: <term d="A loop where the response amplifies the original change, pushing it further until an end point is reached.">Positive feedback</term>
blocks.def: Occurs when a change in a controlled variable triggers a response that AMPLIFIES that same change — pushing the variable further away from normal, not back toward it. It is stimulatory, brings about disequilibrium, and is NOT generally involved in maintaining homeostasis. However, positive feedback can occasionally make negative feedback more efficient in specific contexts. Simple analogy: a microphone feeding back into its own speaker, getting louder and louder rather than settling down.

blocks.name: Feedforward control
blocks.def: A response made in ANTICIPATION of a change in a controlled variable — the disturbance is suppressed before it even has the chance to affect the system's essential variables. It is not error-based (it doesn't wait for something to go wrong first), prepares the body for a change, improves the speed of homeostatic responses, and minimizes fluctuations. Such regulation relies on external detectors or learned associations.

blocks.name: Examples of feedforward control
blocks.def: The salivation reflex (mouth waters at the sight/smell of food, before eating starts), insulin secretion triggered by food merely entering the gut, penile erection triggered by visual or tactile stimuli, shivering that begins before dipping into cold water, and increases in heart and respiratory rate that occur before a stressful or exertional event even begins. In every case, the body reacts to a PREDICTED need, not an actual measured deviation.

sections.title: Signal Transduction — How Cells Hear the Message

items: Control loops need messages, and cells have no eyes or ears — they read the world chemically, through receptors.
Four stages, and they map onto a phone call: reception (the phone rings), transduction (you understand what is said), response (you act), termination (you hang up).
Termination is not an afterthought. A signal that cannot be switched off is as dangerous as one that never arrives — many diseases and drugs act right here.

Where the receptor sits is decided by whether the messenger can cross the oily membrane (Topic 01): fat-soluble messengers (steroids, thyroid hormone) go inside to intracellular receptors; water-soluble ones (adrenaline, insulin) must knock at the surface.
Surface receptors come in three flavours: channel-linked (fastest — milliseconds), catalytic/enzyme-linked, and G-protein-coupled (the most common drug target of all).
Amplification is the payoff: one hormone molecule at the surface can end up changing thousands of molecules inside. A whisper at the door becomes a shout inside the house.
A near-miss in traffic: within a second your heart is pounding — a tiny amount of adrenaline, amplified into a whole-body response.
Antihistamines, beta-blockers, salbutamol inhalers and most common drugs work by blocking or activating a receptor — nearly all of modern pharmacology lives in this section.

blocks.x: A <term d="A chemical messenger released into the blood that acts on distant target tissues.">hormone</term> floating in the blood can't just walk into a cell and flip a switch. Instead, it knocks on the door (binds a <term d="A protein that recognises and binds a specific signal molecule, triggering a response in the cell.">receptor</term>), and that knock triggers a whole relay race of molecular messengers inside the cell until, eventually, something actually happens — a gene turns on, an enzyme activates. That relay race is signal transduction.

blocks.name: Signal transduction (cell signaling)
blocks.def: A cascade of processes that convert an extracellular stimulus into an intracellular response, allowing a cell to adapt to its changing environment. In signal transduction, a cell converts one kind of signal into another, typically through an ordered sequence of biochemical reactions called the transduction pathway.

blocks.name: Why signal transduction matters medically
blocks.def: It controls and maintains normal physiological balance in the body. Many diseases — diabetes, heart disease, autoimmunity, and cancer — arise from defects in signal transduction pathways, which is exactly why this topic is central to modern drug discovery.

blocks.name: Four stages of signal transduction
blocks.def: Reception, Transduction, Response, and Termination — in that order. Every signaling pathway, no matter how complex, follows this same four-step shape.

blocks.name: Reception (Recognition)
blocks.def: The detection of an external signal by a cell, through the interaction between a messenger (<term d="Any molecule that binds to a receptor to deliver a signal.">ligand</term>) and a receptor — the 'knock on the door.'

blocks.name: Transduction (the stage, not the whole process)
blocks.def: The conversion of the received signal into other signals, via alteration of the receptor protein, which triggers off a cascade of reactions — the signal transduction pathway proper.

blocks.name: Response
blocks.def: The transduction pathway triggers an actual response: turning on a gene, activating an enzyme, or rearranging the cytoskeleton. There is usually amplification of the signal at this stage — a small stimulus becomes a big effect.

blocks.name: Termination
blocks.def: The cessation of the generated response, achieved through several possible mechanisms: falling concentration of the first messenger (due to metabolism/<term d="Movement of particles from an area where they are crowded to where they are sparse, until evenly spread.">diffusion</term>), protein phosphatases removing phosphate tags, regeneration of G proteins, phosphodiesterases breaking down cAMP, receptor phosphorylation, uncoupling of receptor-effector molecules, receptor sequestration (internalization), and receptor desensitization. The signal must be actively switched OFF, or it would run forever.

blocks.title: Next up — where the receptor sits decides everything

items: One question sorts this whole block: can the messenger cross the oily membrane?
Fat-soluble (steroids, thyroid hormone) → walks in → intracellular receptor → usually changes gene transcription → slow but long-lasting.
Water-soluble (adrenaline, insulin) → cannot enter → must use a surface receptor → fast but short-lived.

blocks.name: Receptors (general properties)
blocks.def: Receptors are specific (they respond to particular ligands), subject to physiological regulation, and may be either intracellular or membrane-bound.

blocks.name: Intracellular receptors
blocks.def: Receptors located inside the cell (cytoplasmic or nuclear). To use these, the ligand itself must physically cross the cell membrane and bind the receptor inside — meaning only molecules that can cross the lipid bilayer can use this route. These ligands are usually lipophilic (fat-soluble): steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone, progesterone), thyroid hormones (T3, T4), vitamin D, and retinoic acid.

blocks.name: What intracellular receptors do once activated
blocks.def: Upon ligand binding, the receptor migrates to the nucleus, where the ligand-receptor complex binds directly to a region of DNA and affects gene transcription — this is why steroid hormone effects tend to be slow-onset but long-lasting, since they work by changing which genes are being read.

blocks.name: Why hydrophilic hormones can't use intracellular receptors
blocks.def: Hydrophilic molecules like insulin and adrenaline cannot cross the lipid membrane, so they are forced to use cell-surface receptors instead — a direct consequence of the 'like dissolves like' rule of the lipid bilayer.

blocks.title: Next up — the three types of surface receptor

items: Channel-linked — the fastest (milliseconds). The receptor is the ion channel. Used where speed matters: synapses.
Catalytic (enzyme-linked) — the receptor becomes an enzyme. Slower, used for growth and metabolism (e.g. insulin).
G-protein-coupled — the middle ground, and by far the most common — the target of a large share of all medicines.

blocks.name: Cell surface receptors (general)
blocks.def: Integral transmembrane proteins that recognize the vast majority of extracellular signaling molecules. Signal transduction occurs when a stimulatory ligand binds the receptor's EXTRACELLULAR domain — the ligand itself never crosses the membrane. There are three major classes: channel-linked receptors, catalytic receptors, and G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).

blocks.name: Channel-linked receptors
blocks.def: Receptors directly linked to ion channels, whose conductance is modulated by agonist or antagonist binding. They are fast-acting, and directly transduce a chemical signal (from a <term d="A chemical messenger released by a nerve cell to pass a signal across a synapse.">neurotransmitter</term>) into an electrical signal — when the neurotransmitter binds, the receptor's shape changes to open or close the channel immediately.

blocks.name: Catalytic receptors
blocks.def: Transmembrane proteins with an extracellular receptor domain and an intracellular domain that serves as (or is associated with) an enzyme, connected by a single hydrophobic alpha helix. Ligand binding to a single chain alone causes no conformational change — instead, ligand occupancy causes DIMERIZATION (two receptor molecules pairing up), and it's this pairing that triggers the conformational change and downstream signaling.

blocks.name: Examples mediated by catalytic receptors
blocks.def: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and nitric oxide (NO) work via receptor guanylyl cyclases; transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) works via receptor serine/threonine kinases; epidermal growth factor (EGF), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and insulin work via receptor tyrosine kinases; interleukins work via tyrosine kinase-associated receptors.

blocks.title: Next up — GPCRs, step by step

items: The logic never changes: messenger binds → G protein activated → effector enzyme switched on → second messenger made → response.
Gs stimulates, Gi inhibits — the same receptor family can therefore turn a cell up or down.
G proteins switch themselves off on a timer, which is why the signal ends by itself.
Do not memorise these as separate facts — it is one relay chain, and each definition is one link.

blocks.name: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)
blocks.def: Transmembrane proteins that wind back and forth through the <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">plasma</term> membrane 7 times, coupled to membrane-bound enzymes or ion channels via G proteins. The ligand-binding site is exposed outside the cell; the effector site extends into the cytosol. Binding of ligand activates an associated G protein, which then couples the receptor to downstream ion channels or enzymes.

blocks.cap: The GPCR signaling relay: ligand → receptor → G protein → enzyme → <term d="A molecule made inside the cell that relays a signal received at the surface to the cell's machinery.">second messenger</term> → response.

blocks.name: G proteins (guanine nucleotide-binding proteins)
blocks.def: Molecules that couple receptors to membrane-bound channels and enzymes such as adenylate cyclase. The inactive form consists of alpha, beta, and gamma subunits with GDP bound to the alpha subunit; the beta-gamma pair anchors the whole complex to the membrane. Normally free-floating in the membrane, not permanently bound to the receptor.

blocks.name: How GPCR activation works, step by step
blocks.def: Agonist binding to the receptor enhances the receptor's guanine-nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) activity, causing the alpha subunit to swap its GDP for GTP. The G protein then releases from the receptor and splits into an active alpha-GTP subunit and a beta-gamma pair — these two pieces go on to trigger the actual effector interactions (activating enzymes or channels).

blocks.name: How G proteins switch themselves back off
blocks.def: The alpha subunit has its own intrinsic GTPase activity, which hydrolyzes GTP back to GDP, returning the G protein to its inactive state, at which point alpha-GDP and beta-gamma can recombine. 'Regulator of G-protein signaling' (RGS) proteins accelerate this GTP hydrolysis — this accelerating activity is called GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity.

blocks.name: Stimulatory vs inhibitory G proteins
blocks.def: G proteins can be stimulatory (Gs, which activate their effector) or inhibitory (Gi, which inhibit their effector) — the same basic mechanism can either turn a pathway up or down depending on which type of G protein is involved.

blocks.name: Effectors of G proteins
blocks.def: Enzymes such as adenylyl cyclases, phospholipases, phosphodiesterases, kinases, and ion channels — G proteins ultimately act on this range of downstream targets to produce the cell's response.

blocks.name: How GPCR signaling gets turned off
blocks.def: Several mechanisms cooperate: inactivation of the G protein itself; phosphorylation of the receptor by a kinase (which reduces the receptor's ability to respond to its ligand and recruits a protein called β-arrestin, which further desensitizes the receptor); and triggering the breakdown of the GPCR's second messengers.

blocks.title: Next up — how the message spreads inside

items: The first messenger never enters. Second messengers carry the news inside the cell.
cAMP and cGMP — made from ATP/GTP, they activate protein kinases.
IP₃ and DAG — one splits into two: IP₃ releases calcium from stores, DAG stays in the membrane. They work as a team.
Calcium and calmodulin — the pair you meet again in smooth muscle (Topic 06).
This is where amplification happens: one messenger outside → thousands of molecules changed inside.

blocks.name: Second messengers (overview)
blocks.def: Molecules that relay signals received at cell-surface receptors to target molecules in the cytosol and/or nucleus. There are three major classes: cyclic nucleotides (cAMP and cGMP), inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), and calcium ions (Ca2+).

blocks.name: Cyclic AMP (cAMP)
blocks.def: Synthesized from ATP by the enzyme adenylyl cyclase. Hormone binding to its receptor activates a G protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase, which produces cAMP. cAMP then either activates Protein Kinase A (PKA — a cAMP-dependent kinase that phosphorylates target proteins) or directly turns on new gene transcription. cAMP activity is terminated when cAMP-phosphodiesterase converts it to 5'-AMP.

blocks.name: Cyclic GMP (cGMP)
blocks.def: Synthesized from GTP by the enzyme guanylyl cyclase. cGMP serves as the second messenger for atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and nitric oxide (NO). Its effects are mediated through Protein Kinase G (PKG), a cGMP-dependent kinase. cGMP activity is terminated when cGMP-phosphodiesterase converts it to 5'-GMP.

blocks.x: ▶️Phospholipase C, IP3 and DAGVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: IP3 and DAG — where they come from
blocks.def: Both are synthesized from phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), a lipid found in the inner layer of the plasma membrane. Ligand binding to a GPCR activates phospholipase C (PLC), a membrane-bound enzyme, which hydrolyzes (splits) PIP2 into two products: IP3 and DAG. One lipid, split in two, gives rise to two completely different second messengers.

blocks.name: IP3 (inositol trisphosphate) — the water-soluble messenger
blocks.def: Being water-soluble, IP3 diffuses through the cytoplasm to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it binds IP3 receptors on the ER membrane. This causes Ca2+ to be released from the ER into the cytosol, and this rise in intracellular Ca2+ triggers downstream processes such as muscle contraction, exocytosis (e.g., insulin release), and enzyme activation.

blocks.name: DAG (diacylglycerol) — the lipid-soluble messenger
blocks.def: Being lipid-soluble, DAG stays put in the cell membrane (it cannot diffuse into the watery cytosol like IP3 can). It works together with Ca2+ (released via IP3's action) to activate Protein Kinase C (PKC). PKC then phosphorylates many proteins, producing changes in metabolism, secretion, growth, and gene expression.

blocks.name: Why IP3 and DAG work as a team
blocks.def: IP3 releases Ca2+ from the ER; DAG activates PKC; and the released Ca2+ together with DAG synergize to strongly activate PKC and other calcium-dependent enzymes. Net result: a single receptor-binding event, via one split lipid, produces a powerful and versatile cellular response — especially for contraction, secretion, and growth.

blocks.name: Calcium ions (Ca2+) as second messengers
blocks.def: Probably the most widely used intracellular messenger of all. The cell has two main depots of Ca2+ to draw from: the extracellular fluid, and the endoplasmic reticulum (called the '<term d="The muscle cell's internal calcium store, released to trigger contraction.">sarcoplasmic reticulum</term>' specifically in skeletal muscle).

blocks.name: Calmodulin
blocks.def: An intracellular calcium-binding protein. Once Ca2+ enters the cytosol (through Ca2+ channels), it binds to calmodulin — specifically, four Ca2+ ions bind to every one calmodulin molecule. The resulting Ca2+-calmodulin complex then triggers many types of cellular responses, including secretion, contraction, and enzyme activation.

blocks.name: Signal amplification
blocks.def: In many signal transduction pathways, the initial signal triggers a cascading effect that amplifies itself — the number of participating molecules increases at each stage as the process moves further from the initial stimulus, and each stage can amplify the effect hundreds of times over. The net result: a single messenger molecule binding a single receptor can ultimately cause the production of a million downstream product molecules. This is exactly why a tiny hormone concentration in the blood can still produce a large, body-wide effect.

sections.title: Classic Examples of Homeostasis in Action

items: Temperature: skin and hypothalamic sensors → hypothalamus compares to ~37 °C → sweating and vessel widening to lose heat, or shivering and vessel narrowing to keep it. Negative feedback.

Blood glucose: rises after a meal → pancreas releases insulin → cells take sugar in and the liver stores it → glucose falls. When it drops too low, glucagon does the reverse. Negative feedback with two opposing hands.
Blood pressure: baroreceptors sense a fall → the brainstem responds → heart rate and vessel tone rise → pressure recovers. Negative feedback, in seconds.
Childbirth: contractions push the baby down → stretch triggers oxytocin → contractions get stronger. Positive feedback — and it ends only when the baby is delivered.
Clotting: each clotting factor activates more of the next, so a small cut seals fast. Again positive feedback with a natural end point.
Why positive feedback is rare: it is a runaway process by design. The body uses it only when it needs a job finished decisively, and only when something will stop it.
Feeling shaky, sweaty and irritable when a meal is very late — that is glucose regulation being pushed to its limits.
The dizziness when you stand up too fast is the blood-pressure loop caught half a second late; it passes as soon as the baroreceptor reflex catches up.
A cut on your finger stopping on its own in a couple of minutes is positive feedback doing exactly what it should.

blocks.x: Reading the definitions is one thing — seeing homeostasis actually work is what makes it click. These are the textbook examples every physiology student should be able to walk through step by step.

blocks.name: Thermoregulation as negative feedback
blocks.def: Body temperature is a controlled variable. If temperature rises above the <term d="The target value the body defends, like the temperature setting on a thermostat.">set point</term>, detectors (thermoreceptors) signal the hypothalamus (the control center), which triggers effectors: sweating and blood vessel dilation to lose heat. If temperature falls, the same system triggers shivering and blood vessel constriction to conserve/generate heat. Either direction, the response OPPOSES the original change — classic negative feedback.

blocks.name: Blood glucose regulation as negative feedback
blocks.def: After a meal, rising blood glucose is detected by the pancreas, which releases insulin, causing cells to take up glucose and lowering blood glucose back toward normal. When blood glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases glucagon instead, which raises blood glucose back up. Two hormones, opposite directions, same goal: keep glucose in a narrow range.

blocks.name: Blood pressure regulation as negative feedback
blocks.def: Baroreceptors (pressure sensors) in the walls of major blood vessels detect a rise or fall in blood pressure and send signals to the cardiovascular control center in the brainstem, which adjusts heart rate and blood vessel diameter to bring pressure back toward normal.

blocks.name: Childbirth (labor contractions) as positive feedback
blocks.def: The classic physiological example of positive feedback: stretching of the cervix stimulates contractions, which push the baby further against the cervix, causing MORE stretching, and therefore MORE contractions — the response amplifies the original stimulus rather than opposing it, and the cycle only ends with delivery, not with a return to the starting state.

blocks.name: Blood clotting as positive feedback
blocks.def: Another classic positive feedback loop: once clotting begins, activated clotting factors activate even more clotting factors, rapidly amplifying the response until a clot has fully formed — a runaway cascade by design, since a slow, hesitant clotting response would be dangerous during active bleeding.

blocks.name: Why the body uses positive feedback sparingly
blocks.def: Because positive feedback drives a variable further from its starting point rather than restoring balance, it is inherently self-limiting or dangerous if left unchecked — which is why the body reserves it for situations with a natural, hard endpoint (like delivery of a baby, or a completed clot), rather than for ongoing regulation of everyday variables like temperature or glucose.

items: S–C–E: Sensor → Control centre → Effector. Every loop in physiology, without exception.
Negative opposes, positive amplifies, feedforward anticipates.
Fat-soluble goes in; water-soluble knocks. That decides intracellular vs surface receptor every time.
Four stages: reception → transduction → response → termination (ring → understand → act → hang up).

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: 'Negative feedback' does not mean harmful. Negative describes the direction of the correction, not its value — it is the body's most useful mechanism.
Positive feedback is not a malfunction. Labour and clotting use it deliberately, because both need a decisive finish.
Homeostasis is not 'no change'. It is constant small change, constantly corrected.
'Transduction' has two meanings here — the whole process, and one stage within it. Let the sentence tell you which.
← Body Fluids (Topic 01): the internal environment being defended is the ECF, and its volume and composition are what these loops are actually protecting.
→ Excitable Tissues (Topic 03) & Communication Between Cells (Topic 07): the sensors and messengers here are nerves and synapses — the fast branch of the same control machinery.
→ Autonomic Nervous System (Topic 09): the ANS is homeostasis's field team. Its receptors are the exact receptor types you met in signal transduction, and the hypothalamus sets its balance.
The one-line summary: sensor → control centre → effector, repeated everywhere. Once you spot the loop, every regulatory topic becomes the same story with new characters.

lines: Negative feedback returns a variable towards its set point and runs almost everything; positive feedback drives a process to completion and is rare.
Clotting, labour and the pre-ovulatory LH surge — if an exam asks for positive feedback, these are the safe answers.
Every reflex arc is the same three parts: something senses the change, something compares it to the set point, something acts to correct it.
Homeostasis holds variables within a narrow range around a set point that can itself be reset — fever is the thermostat moved, not broken.
